total_gdp.meaning: Gross domestic product (GDP) is the monetary value of final goods and services produced inside an economy during a period. Here it is an annual flow of production, including public services; intermediate inputs are not counted again as final products. It is not the amount of money held by the country, its accumulated wealth, or government revenue.
total_gdp.calculation: National accounts can add value created by producers, add income generated by production, or add household/private final consumption + investment + government consumption + exports − imports. Imports are deducted because they are foreign production already included in spending. In this Atlas, Total GDP is calculated from compatible GDP per person × population for the same year and source; population stored in thousands is first multiplied by 1,000. The displayed 2011 international dollars are purchasing-power units, not the exchange-rate dollars of that historical year.
total_gdp.interpretation: Higher total GDP means more annual economic output. A populous country can have a large total while output per person remains low. Lower GDP means less output, not necessarily poorer households or lower wellbeing. Distribution, unpaid work, environmental damage and many aspects of quality of life are not captured by this total.

gdp.meaning: GDP per person is annual economic output within a country divided by its population: an average amount of production per resident. It is not a typical wage, household income, or the money each resident receives.
gdp.calculation: GDP per person = annual GDP ÷ population, using compatible territory and time coverage. This series uses 2011 purchasing-power-parity international dollars: a common purchasing-power price basis for comparisons, rather than each year’s market exchange rate. Historical values can be reconstructed estimates. Any interpolation or calculation used for the selected observation is described separately.
gdp.interpretation: Higher values indicate more average output per person, which can support higher material living standards. They do not reveal who receives the income, how expensive a particular household’s basket is, or overall wellbeing. Lower values indicate less output per person; compare only compatible price bases and definitions.

trade_balance.meaning: Trade balance is the value of exports minus imports. This indicator includes both goods and services and expresses their net balance relative to the size of the economy.
trade_balance.calculation: Trade balance (% of GDP) = 100 × (exports − imports) ÷ GDP. The Atlas subtracts the published imports share from the exports share for the same country, year and compatible scope. For example, exports of 30% of GDP and imports of 35% give −5% of GDP. Merchandise-only partner totals have a different scope and are shown separately.
trade_balance.interpretation: Positive means a surplus: exports exceed imports. Negative means a deficit: imports exceed exports. Zero means they balance. A higher value is a larger surplus or smaller deficit; a lower value is the reverse. A surplus is not automatically good, nor a deficit automatically bad. This is not the current account, which also includes primary income and transfers.

sources.title: World Bank: Balance of goods and services

exports.meaning: Exports of goods and services are products and services supplied by residents of an economy to non-residents. This measure shows their value relative to annual GDP.
exports.calculation: Exports share = 100 × exports of goods and services ÷ GDP for the same period, using compatible national-accounts values. Gross exports include imported inputs that may later be re-exported, so the share can exceed 100%.
exports.interpretation: Higher means exports are large relative to domestic output; lower means a smaller export share. Neither alone indicates prosperity or a trade surplus: imports, domestic value added, prices and economic structure also matter.

sources.title: World Bank: Balance of goods and services

imports.meaning: Imports of goods and services are products and services supplied by non-residents to residents of an economy. This measure shows their value relative to annual GDP.
imports.calculation: Imports share = 100 × imports of goods and services ÷ GDP for the same period. It includes consumer products, production inputs, equipment and services. Imports are subtracted in GDP accounting to remove foreign production, not because importing itself destroys value.
imports.interpretation: Higher means imports are large relative to domestic output; lower means a smaller import share. A high share can reflect access to useful goods, supply-chain integration or dependence on external suppliers. It does not by itself establish a deficit or economic weakness.

pop.meaning: Population counts people in the area and population group specified by the series. The urban-China series counts urban residents only; the former-south Morocco series covers that source region, not the whole modern country.
pop.calculation: Sources count residents through censuses or estimate them using demographic records and reconstruction. The core series is a mid-year population estimate stored in thousands; the interface converts it to people. Other series retain their stated benchmark date and territorial scope. This is a count, not a population density.
pop.interpretation: Higher means more people within the specified area and scope, not inherently better or worse living conditions. Changes can reflect births, deaths, migration, changing boundaries or revised estimates. Compare consistent territorial definitions; regional and urban counts are not national totals.

population_density.meaning: Population density is the average number of people per square kilometre of land area. It describes how concentrated the population is across a territory.
population_density.calculation: Density = mid-year population ÷ land area in square kilometres; inland water is excluded in this source. It is an area-wide average, not a measurement of crowding in each town or neighbourhood.
population_density.interpretation: Higher means more residents per unit of land; lower means fewer. Neither is intrinsically good or bad. A country with deserts and a few dense cities can have a low national average despite urban crowding. Population totals and density answer different questions.

life.meaning: Life expectancy at birth is how many years a newborn would live on average if the age-specific death rates of the stated period continued throughout that child’s life. It summarises mortality conditions at that time.
life.calculation: A life table applies death probabilities at successive ages to a hypothetical birth cohort. The total years that cohort would live are divided by the number of births. It is not the average age of people currently alive or a prediction that future mortality will stay unchanged; historical reconstructions may use incomplete records and models.
life.interpretation: Higher generally indicates lower mortality and longer expected lives under that period’s conditions; lower indicates higher mortality. Infant mortality, epidemics, conflict and adult deaths can all affect the figure. Small changes in estimated series may be uncertain.

historical_life.meaning: Life expectancy at birth is how many years a newborn would live on average if the age-specific death rates of the stated period continued throughout that child’s life. It summarises mortality conditions at that time.
historical_life.calculation: A life table applies death probabilities at successive ages to a hypothetical birth cohort. The total years that cohort would live are divided by the number of births. It is not the average age of people currently alive or a prediction that future mortality will stay unchanged; historical reconstructions may use incomplete records and models.
historical_life.interpretation: Higher generally indicates lower mortality and longer expected lives under that period’s conditions; lower indicates higher mortality. Infant mortality, epidemics, conflict and adult deaths can all affect the figure. Small changes in estimated series may be uncertain.

hdi.meaning: The Human Development Index (HDI) summarises average achievement in health, education and material living standards on a scale from 0 to 1.
hdi.calculation: UNDP combines a life-expectancy index, an education index built from mean and expected years of schooling, and an income index based on the logarithm of purchasing-power-adjusted gross national income per person. The HDI is the geometric mean of the three dimension indices. The Atlas displays UNDP’s published values, not a new calculation from the visible GDP series.
hdi.interpretation: Higher means higher combined achievement in these three dimensions; lower means lower achievement. HDI is not a percentage of people doing well and does not itself describe inequality, political freedom or environmental sustainability.

school_mean.meaning: Mean years of schooling measures the average completed years of formal education in the stated adult population. The modern series covers ages 25 and older; the historical series covers ages 15 and older.
school_mean.calculation: Survey or census educational attainment is converted into completed schooling years and averaged across the relevant population, including people with no formal schooling. Published historical estimates retain their own reconstruction methods and benchmark periods.
school_mean.interpretation: Higher means the specified adult population completed more schooling on average. Lower means fewer completed years. This does not directly measure learning quality, literacy or current school attendance. The age-15+ and age-25+ series are not interchangeable.

historical_schooling.meaning: Mean years of schooling measures the average completed years of formal education in the stated adult population. The modern series covers ages 25 and older; the historical series covers ages 15 and older.
historical_schooling.calculation: Survey or census educational attainment is converted into completed schooling years and averaged across the relevant population, including people with no formal schooling. Published historical estimates retain their own reconstruction methods and benchmark periods.
historical_schooling.interpretation: Higher means the specified adult population completed more schooling on average. Lower means fewer completed years. This does not directly measure learning quality, literacy or current school attendance. The age-15+ and age-25+ series are not interchangeable.

school_expected.meaning: Expected years of schooling is the number of years of education a child entering school could expect if the current pattern of age-specific enrolment continued.
school_expected.calculation: Enrolment rates at successive ages are added across the education system under the source’s conventions. This is an expectation based on current enrolment, not the completed education of today’s adults or a promise about a particular child.
school_expected.interpretation: Higher generally indicates broader or longer participation in education; lower indicates fewer expected years. It does not directly measure learning outcomes or completion, and should not be confused with mean years already completed.

happiness.meaning: Life evaluation records how people rate their own lives on the Cantril ladder, from 0 (worst possible life) to 10 (best possible life). This series is a published three-year average.
happiness.calculation: Survey respondents choose a ladder score. The source combines survey responses using its weighting and multi-year averaging procedures. The displayed year is the window’s end; actual survey coverage can vary. The score is not calculated from GDP, health or other Atlas indicators.
happiness.interpretation: Higher means respondents evaluated their lives more favourably on average; lower means less favourably. It is not the percentage of happy people. Survey uncertainty, cultural response patterns and differences within the population matter.

gini.meaning: The Gini index summarises how unequally income or consumption is distributed. In this Atlas it uses 0 for complete equality and 100 for maximum inequality in the usual nonnegative-income setting.
gini.calculation: Order people or households from poorest to richest and compare their cumulative share of income or consumption with an equal distribution (the Lorenz curve). The Gini is the gap between these curves relative to the maximum gap, expressed on a 0–100 scale. Published survey weights and household definitions matter; the historical series specifically concerns gross household income.
gini.interpretation: Higher means more unequal distribution; lower means more equal distribution. It does not show average living standards or poverty: a poor society can be relatively equal. Income, consumption, gross-income and net-income series should not be treated as identical.

historical_gini_gross.meaning: The Gini index summarises how unequally income or consumption is distributed. In this Atlas it uses 0 for complete equality and 100 for maximum inequality in the usual nonnegative-income setting.
historical_gini_gross.calculation: Order people or households from poorest to richest and compare their cumulative share of income or consumption with an equal distribution (the Lorenz curve). The Gini is the gap between these curves relative to the maximum gap, expressed on a 0–100 scale. Published survey weights and household definitions matter; the historical series specifically concerns gross household income.
historical_gini_gross.interpretation: Higher means more unequal distribution; lower means more equal distribution. It does not show average living standards or poverty: a poor society can be relatively equal. Income, consumption, gross-income and net-income series should not be treated as identical.

poverty.meaning: The poverty headcount ratio is the percentage of people whose household income or consumption per person is below 3.00 international dollars per day at 2021 purchasing-power prices.
poverty.calculation: Headcount (%) = 100 × people below the 3.00-a-day threshold ÷ total population represented by the survey, using the source’s survey weights and income or consumption measure. Purchasing-power conversion compares buying power; this is not a literal daily US-dollar cash wage.
poverty.interpretation: Higher means a larger share below this poverty line; lower means a smaller share. It does not show how far below the line people are, or the number of poor people without also considering population. Different thresholds and PPP base years cannot be substituted silently.

poverty_lower_middle.meaning: The poverty headcount ratio is the percentage of people whose household income or consumption per person is below 4.20 international dollars per day at 2021 purchasing-power prices.
poverty_lower_middle.calculation: Headcount (%) = 100 × people below the 4.20-a-day threshold ÷ total population represented by the survey, using the source’s survey weights and income or consumption measure. poverty_lower_middle.interpretation: Higher means a larger share below this poverty line; lower means a smaller share. electricity.meaning: This measures the percentage of people with electricity. The qualifying condition is access to an electricity connection or supply as defined in the source.
electricity.calculation: Share (%) = 100 × people meeting the service definition ÷ population represented. Sources combine surveys, censuses and administrative evidence using their stated estimation methods.
electricity.interpretation: Higher means more widespread access or use; lower means less. Access alone does not establish affordability, reliability, safety beyond the stated service level, or equal access for every community.

water.meaning: This measures the percentage of people with at least basic drinking water. The qualifying condition is an improved drinking-water source reachable within a round trip of 30 minutes, including queuing; safely managed services are included.
water.calculation: Share (%) = 100 × people meeting the service definition ÷ population represented. Sources combine surveys, censuses and administrative evidence using their stated estimation methods.
water.interpretation: Higher means more widespread access or use; lower means less. Access alone does not establish affordability, reliability, safety beyond the stated service level, or equal access for every community.

sanitation.meaning: This measures the percentage of people with at least basic sanitation. The qualifying condition is an improved sanitation facility not shared with other households; safely managed services are included.
sanitation.calculation: Share (%) = 100 × people meeting the service definition ÷ population represented. Sources combine surveys, censuses and administrative evidence using their stated estimation methods.
sanitation.interpretation: Higher means more widespread access or use; lower means less. Access alone does not establish affordability, reliability, safety beyond the stated service level, or equal access for every community.

internet.meaning: This measures the percentage of people with the Internet. The qualifying condition is Internet use from any location during the preceding three months.

birth_rate.meaning: The crude birth rate counts live births during a year relative to the total population, expressed per 1,000 people.
birth_rate.calculation: Birth rate = 1,000 × live births during the year ÷ mid-year population. Historical series retain the published rate and its coverage, rather than silently recalculating from inconsistent surviving counts.
birth_rate.interpretation: Higher means more births relative to population; lower means fewer. This is not births per woman (the fertility rate). Age structure and the share of women of childbearing age affect it, so neither direction alone measures wellbeing.

death_rate.meaning: The crude death rate counts deaths during a year relative to the total population, expressed per 1,000 people.
death_rate.calculation: Death rate = 1,000 × deaths during the year ÷ mid-year population. It is not adjusted for age composition. Historical rates retain their published coverage and reconstruction notes.
death_rate.interpretation: Higher means more deaths relative to population; lower means fewer. An older population can have a higher crude rate despite better health care, so it is not a simple cross-country health ranking. Age-specific mortality and life expectancy provide additional context.

infant_mortality.meaning: This mortality measure describes deaths before age one year, expressed per 1,000 live births. It concerns survival early in life, not deaths per 1,000 total residents.
infant_mortality.calculation: The source estimates the probability that a live-born child dies before age one year, expressed × 1,000, or reports a vital-registration rate from deaths and live births under its historical convention. Life-table methods, survey models and simple registered ratios are not identical. Historical decade estimates remain labelled as period estimates rather than independent annual counts.
infant_mortality.interpretation: Higher indicates worse survival; lower indicates better survival. A value of 50 per 1,000 corresponds to roughly 5 deaths per 100 live births under the stated definition. Registration completeness, model uncertainty and period coverage matter.

agriculture_share.meaning: This is the share of the economy’s annual output contributed by agriculture, forestry and fishing, measured as value added.
agriculture_share.calculation: Share (% of GDP) = 100 × sector value added ÷ total GDP at compatible current prices. Value added is output minus the goods and services used up in producing it. Manufacturing is part of industry: do not add both as separate non-overlapping sectors. Classification and product-tax treatment can mean displayed shares do not sum exactly to 100%.
agriculture_share.interpretation: Higher means the sector accounts for a larger share of output, not necessarily that it is more productive or people are richer. A share can fall while the sector grows if other sectors grow faster. This is not its share of jobs or exports.

industry_share.meaning: This is the share of the economy’s annual output contributed by industry, including manufacturing, mining, utilities and construction, measured as value added.
industry_share.calculation: Share (% of GDP) = 100 × sector value added ÷ total GDP at compatible current prices. Value added is output minus the goods and services used up in producing it. Manufacturing is part of industry: do not add both as separate non-overlapping sectors. Classification and product-tax treatment can mean displayed shares do not sum exactly to 100%.
industry_share.interpretation: Higher means the sector accounts for a larger share of output, not necessarily that it is more productive or people are richer. A share can fall while the sector grows if other sectors grow faster. This is not its share of jobs or exports.

manufacturing_share.meaning: This is the share of the economy’s annual output contributed by manufacturing, the transformation of materials into products, measured as value added.
manufacturing_share.calculation: Share (% of GDP) = 100 × sector value added ÷ total GDP at compatible current prices. Value added is output minus the goods and services used up in producing it. Manufacturing is part of industry: do not add both as separate non-overlapping sectors. Classification and product-tax treatment can mean displayed shares do not sum exactly to 100%.
manufacturing_share.interpretation: Higher means the sector accounts for a larger share of output, not necessarily that it is more productive or people are richer. A share can fall while the sector grows if other sectors grow faster. This is not its share of jobs or exports.

services_share.meaning: This is the share of the economy’s annual output contributed by service activities, such as trade, transport, finance, education and health, measured as value added.
services_share.calculation: Share (% of GDP) = 100 × sector value added ÷ total GDP at compatible current prices. Value added is output minus the goods and services used up in producing it. Manufacturing is part of industry: do not add both as separate non-overlapping sectors. Classification and product-tax treatment can mean displayed shares do not sum exactly to 100%.
services_share.interpretation: Higher means the sector accounts for a larger share of output, not necessarily that it is more productive or people are richer. A share can fall while the sector grows if other sectors grow faster. This is not its share of jobs or exports.

defence_spending_eur.meaning: Government defence expenditure is public spending classified under the defence function in the Eurostat government accounts. It includes more than the cost of a particular war and uses a specific accounting scope.
defence_spending_eur.calculation: The source totals general-government expenditure assigned to COFOG defence under ESA 2010. The amount series is in current euros; the GDP-share series divides this annual expenditure by the same year’s GDP and multiplies by 100. Any currency or inflation conversion in the display is a separate calculation.
defence_spending_eur.interpretation: Higher amounts mean more spending under this definition; higher GDP shares mean a larger spending burden relative to annual output. Neither directly measures combat effectiveness, security or a war’s total social cost. A lower share can result from GDP growth even if spending increases.

defence_spending_gdp.meaning: Government defence expenditure is public spending classified under the defence function in the Eurostat government accounts. It includes more than the cost of a particular war and uses a specific accounting scope.
defence_spending_gdp.calculation: The source totals general-government expenditure assigned to COFOG defence under ESA 2010. The amount series is in current euros; the GDP-share series divides this annual expenditure by the same year’s GDP and multiplies by 100. Any currency or inflation conversion in the display is a separate calculation.
defence_spending_gdp.interpretation: Higher amounts mean more spending under this definition; higher GDP shares mean a larger spending burden relative to annual output. Neither directly measures combat effectiveness, security or a war’s total social cost. A lower share can result from GDP growth even if spending increases.

wealth_bottom20.meaning: This is the share of total household net wealth held by the bottom 20% of households, ranked by wealth. Net wealth is assets minus liabilities; it is a stock at the survey date, not annual income.
wealth_bottom20.calculation: Wealth share (%) = 100 × net wealth of the bottom 20% ÷ total household net wealth, using the survey’s weights and asset coverage. This source excludes employment-related and social-security pension entitlements. Negative net wealth and negative group shares are possible.
wealth_bottom20.interpretation: Higher top-group shares indicate more wealth concentrated at the top; higher bottom-group shares indicate that poorer households hold more of the total. A share does not reveal the group’s wealth in currency units. Wealth surveys may miss wealthy households; definitions and survey dates affect comparisons.

wealth_bottom40.meaning: This is the share of total household net wealth held by the bottom 40% of households, ranked by wealth. Net wealth is assets minus liabilities; it is a stock at the survey date, not annual income.
wealth_bottom40.calculation: Wealth share (%) = 100 × net wealth of the bottom 40% ÷ total household net wealth, using the survey’s weights and asset coverage. This source excludes employment-related and social-security pension entitlements. Negative net wealth and negative group shares are possible.
wealth_bottom40.interpretation: Higher top-group shares indicate more wealth concentrated at the top; higher bottom-group shares indicate that poorer households hold more of the total. A share does not reveal the group’s wealth in currency units. Wealth surveys may miss wealthy households; definitions and survey dates affect comparisons.

wealth_top10.meaning: This is the share of total household net wealth held by the top 10% of households, ranked by wealth. Net wealth is assets minus liabilities; it is a stock at the survey date, not annual income.
wealth_top10.calculation: Wealth share (%) = 100 × net wealth of the top 10% ÷ total household net wealth, using the survey’s weights and asset coverage. This source excludes employment-related and social-security pension entitlements. Negative net wealth and negative group shares are possible.
wealth_top10.interpretation: Higher top-group shares indicate more wealth concentrated at the top; higher bottom-group shares indicate that poorer households hold more of the total. fiscal_debt.meaning: Gross public debt is the outstanding stock of government borrowing obligations at a point in time, expressed relative to annual GDP. It is not the year’s deficit or the debt of every household and business.
fiscal_debt.calculation: Debt-to-GDP (%) = 100 × gross public debt stock ÷ annual GDP. Gross debt is measured before deducting government financial assets. The historical source can use different levels of government and accounting coverage; the observation’s scope remains important.
fiscal_debt.interpretation: Higher means a larger debt stock relative to annual output; lower means a smaller stock. This can change because debt changes or GDP changes. Sustainability also depends on interest costs, currency, maturity, government assets and revenue; there is no universal good/bad threshold.

fiscal_primary_balance.meaning: The primary fiscal balance is government revenue minus spending other than interest payments, expressed as a share of GDP. It shows the budget position before the cost of servicing past debt.
fiscal_primary_balance.calculation: Primary balance (% of GDP) = 100 × (government revenue − non-interest expenditure) ÷ GDP. The Atlas retains the source’s definition and coverage. This differs from the overall budget balance, which includes interest costs.
fiscal_primary_balance.interpretation: Positive means a primary surplus; negative means a primary deficit. Higher means more revenue relative to non-interest spending. It is not automatically better: fiscal needs, the economic cycle, public investment and debt conditions matter.

fiscal_revenue.meaning: Government revenue is the annual inflow recognised as revenue in the fiscal accounts, including taxes and applicable non-tax receipts, expressed relative to GDP.
fiscal_revenue.calculation: Revenue share (%) = 100 × government revenue ÷ annual GDP. Borrowing is financing, not tax or ordinary revenue. Source accounting conventions determine included grants, contributions and other receipts.
fiscal_revenue.interpretation: Higher means the government collects more revenue relative to the economy; lower means less. It does not by itself show efficient taxation, public-service quality or the tax burden on a particular household.

fiscal_expenditure.meaning: Government expenditure is annual public spending under the source’s fiscal-accounting scope, expressed relative to GDP.
fiscal_expenditure.calculation: Expenditure share (%) = 100 × total government expenditure ÷ annual GDP. It can include public services, transfers, interest and investment according to the source; it is not identical to the government-consumption component of GDP.
fiscal_expenditure.interpretation: Higher means more public spending relative to output; lower means less. Neither alone measures waste or good services. Composition, outcomes, revenue and economic conditions determine what the spending implies.

fiscal_interest.meaning: Government interest expenditure is the annual cost of interest on public debt, expressed relative to GDP.
fiscal_interest.calculation: Interest expenditure (% of GDP) = 100 × annual public-debt interest payments ÷ annual GDP. Principal repayments are excluded, so this is not total debt service and not an interest rate.
fiscal_interest.interpretation: Higher means interest costs absorb a larger portion of annual output; lower means a smaller portion. This affects fiscal space, but also depends on debt size, rates and GDP. It should not be confused with the central bank’s policy rate.

fiscal_inflation.meaning: Consumer-price inflation measures how quickly the general price level of the consumer basket changes. It concerns prices faced by consumers, not the growth of GDP or an exchange rate.
fiscal_inflation.calculation: Annual inflation (%) = 100 × (this year’s consumer price index ÷ the previous year’s index − 1), following the source’s annual convention. The CPI combines prices with expenditure weights. A 10% rate means the measured basket costs about 10% more; individual households may experience different price changes.
fiscal_inflation.interpretation: Higher positive inflation means faster price increases; lower positive inflation means prices still rise, but more slowly. Zero means no measured overall change. Negative inflation is deflation: falling prices, which are not automatically beneficial. This differs from expressing historical money in inflation-adjusted dollars.

fiscal_policy_rate.meaning: The central-bank policy rate is the interest rate chosen to represent the monetary authority’s policy stance. The Atlas series records the December end-of-period value.
fiscal_policy_rate.calculation: The BIS selects the official target or administered rate that best represents policy, or the midpoint of a target band where appropriate. The Atlas uses the last business-day December observation and displays it as an annualised percentage; it does not average the full year.
fiscal_policy_rate.interpretation: Higher usually indicates a higher nominal policy borrowing cost; lower a lower cost. This is not a household loan rate, a government bond yield or inflation-adjusted real interest. Negative values are possible, and whether a rate is restrictive depends on inflation and economic conditions.

historical_urbanization.meaning: Urbanization is the share of the population living in places classified as urban by the historical source.
historical_urbanization.calculation: Urban share (%) = 100 × urban population ÷ total population for the same source territory and period. The Atlas converts source fractions to percentages. Definitions of a town or city differ across sources and periods.
historical_urbanization.interpretation: Higher means more residents live in classified urban areas; lower means a more rural population. It is not inherently better or worse, and a change can reflect reclassification as well as migration or population growth.

historical_height.meaning: This measure is reconstructed average adult male-equivalent height for people born in the stated decade. It can provide evidence about childhood nutrition and disease conditions.
historical_height.calculation: Researchers combine historical samples and make source-specific corrections to estimate cohort stature, expressed in centimetres. The date identifies the birth cohort, not the year the adults were measured. The Atlas repeats a decade estimate only within its stated birth decade.
historical_height.interpretation: Higher means taller average adult stature in that cohort; lower means shorter stature. Nutrition, illness, genetics and sample selection all matter. It is not a direct measure of income, health for everyone, or average height of all residents in the selected year.

historical_illiteracy_15_br.meaning: The illiteracy rate is the percentage of people aged 15 and older who do not meet the census definition of being able to read and write.
historical_illiteracy_15_br.calculation: Illiteracy (%) = 100 × people classified as illiterate aged 15+ ÷ population aged 15+, using that census’s classification. The source concerns basic reading and writing rather than functional literacy. Age thresholds are kept separate in the Atlas.
historical_illiteracy_15_br.interpretation: Higher means a larger proportion lacks the measured literacy skills; lower means fewer. Different age cutoffs, census questions and classification practices affect comparability. It is not a school-enrolment rate.

historical_numeracy.meaning: The ABCC numeracy index estimates basic numerical ability from how accurately people reported their ages. Concentration on round-number ages is called age heaping.
historical_numeracy.calculation: Researchers transform a Whipple age-heaping index into the published ABCC scale, generally 0–100. The estimate uses patterns of reported ages rather than a direct arithmetic test. The Atlas keeps source cohort definitions and holds values only within the stated birth decade.
historical_numeracy.interpretation: Higher generally indicates less age heaping and greater inferred basic numeracy; lower indicates more age heaping. It is not a measured literacy percentage, a test score, or years of schooling; registration practices and cultural patterns can also affect reported ages.

historical_gdp_1990.meaning: This is reconstructed annual GDP per person: the value of output per resident, on a 1990 purchasing-power international-dollar basis.
historical_gdp_1990.calculation: Researchers reconstruct annual output and population and express their ratio in the source’s common price and purchasing-power units. It is a published historical model estimate, not a household-income survey. The Atlas does not splice this 1990-price series into its 2011-price GDP series.
historical_gdp_1990.interpretation: Higher means more estimated output per person on this particular price basis; lower means less. It is not a wage or wealth stock. A value cannot be directly compared with an otherwise similar 2011- or 2021-international-dollar amount.

regional_gdp.meaning: This is a calculated allocation of a published region’s annual GDP to its component countries, using population shares. It is an estimate of country output, not a separately observed national total.
regional_gdp.calculation: Allocated country GDP = regional GDP × country population ÷ sum of compatible population estimates for all included regional members. This assumes equal output per person throughout that region. The source uses 1990 international dollars per year; no conversion makes it interchangeable with the 2011-price GDP series.
regional_gdp.interpretation: Higher means a larger allocated output total, usually because of a larger population share or regional total. It does not establish that the country was richer per person. The allocation model and territorial membership must be considered before comparing it with observed national accounts.

hna_fra_agriculture.meaning: This measures the historical share of GDP contributed by agriculture, using the source’s sector definitions and reconstructed national accounts.
hna_fra_agriculture.calculation: Share (% of source GDP) = 100 × sector current-price value added ÷ current-price GDP from the same historical workbook and year. Value added is output minus intermediate inputs. Broad sectors and their component subsectors overlap and must not be added twice.
hna_fra_agriculture.interpretation: Higher means a larger share of the source economy’s output; lower means a smaller share. It does not measure productivity, jobs or purchasing power. A share can change because the rest of the economy changes, and historical classifications may differ from modern ones.

hna_gbr_agriculture_fishing.meaning: This historical agriculture fishing series measures production volume relative to its own 1913 level, set to 100. It is an index of output, not a GDP share or a monetary amount.

hna_gbr_agriculture_fishing.interpretation: Above 100 means more volume than the base year; below 100 means less. A value of 150 means about 50% above that base. Higher index levels across different sectors do not mean one sector produces more money or output in absolute terms.

hna_gbr_construction.interpretation: Above 100 means more volume than the base year; below 100 means less. A value of 150 means about 50% above that base. Higher index levels across different sectors do not mean one sector produces more money or output in absolute terms.

hna_bra_agriculture_fc.meaning: Agriculture and livestock · historical factor-cost share measures the historical share of economic value added in the named activity, using Brazil’s FGV/IBGE consolidated national accounts at factor cost. Value added is output less intermediate inputs, not sales or employment.
hna_bra_agriculture_fc.calculation: The source publishes each activity as a percentage of total factor-cost GDP. Values are retained as printed, with historical classifications and one-decimal rounding.
hna_bra_agriculture_fc.interpretation: Higher means this activity contributed a larger share of the source economy’s output; lower means a smaller share. Neither is inherently better. A falling share can accompany rising production if other activities grow faster. Shares with different price or accounting bases are not directly comparable.

hna_can_agriculture_index.interpretation: Above 100 means more real activity than in 1971; below 100 means less. Higher or lower does not show the size of this sector compared with other countries. Do not add indexes or interpret them as percentages of GDP.

hna_chn_agriculture_ndp1933.meaning: This estimates the contribution of agriculture to mainland China’s net domestic product in the historical 1933 benchmark. NDP excludes depreciation, unlike GDP.
hna_chn_agriculture_ndp1933.calculation: Calculated as 100 × the source sector value ÷ net domestic product of 28.86 billion 1933 yuan. The 13 sector values sum to NDP; depreciation of 1.02 billion is separately added by the source to reach GDP.
hna_chn_agriculture_ndp1933.interpretation: Higher means a larger share of reconstructed net output in 1933. This is not a modern GDP percentage or a welfare ranking. Do not splice it with GDP-share series.

hna_mar_agriculture_durum_wheat_tonnes19.calculation: Source table I reports thousands of metric quintals. The Atlas multiplies each printed quantity by 100 to express metric tonnes. No blank cells are replaced with zero and no missing years are interpolated.
hna_mar_agriculture_durum_wheat_tonnes19.interpretation: Higher means a larger recorded physical quantity of this particular product. Lower means less; it does not by itself mean poorer living standards. Crop failure, weather, coverage and accounting changes can affect the series. Products and processing stages must not be summed as if they were independent value added.

aaowd_wage_bgd_labourer_rupees.meaning: This is the published daily wage for labourer wage · bangladesh, expressed in rupees per paid day (nominal, Bangladesh source). It represents the recorded occupation and locality or payroll scope, not the average income of the whole country.
aaowd_wage_bgd_labourer_rupees.calculation: The compilation expresses pay per paid day in the original currency. Where necessary, authors standardise annual, monthly or hourly pay using 312 days per year, 26 days per month or 8 hours per day, unless the source notes specify otherwise. Source reconstructions and estimates are retained. The Atlas does not multiply this into observed annual household earnings.

aaowd_relative_carpenter_alternative3.interpretation: A value of 2 means twice the comparator wage; 1 means equal pay; below 1 means less. Higher indicates a larger occupational wage premium. It does not establish higher national living standards or a household’s ability to afford essentials.

matched_baskets_beijing.meaning: This is the number of annual family basic-needs baskets that the specified local wage could buy at matched local prices. The basket describes a stated bundle of essentials; it measures that wage’s purchasing power, not GDP per person.
matched_baskets_beijing.calculation: Daily wage × 250 assumed paid days ÷ (annual adult barebones basket × 3.15). The family budget represents three adult equivalents plus 5% rent. Local staple, food, clothing, soap, fuel and light follow the authors’ barebones convention. Source-model uncertainty is not quantified. This is purchasing power of a specified wage against local essentials, not GDP/person, average household income, US dollars or 2011 international dollars. 1× covers one stated annual basket; 0.5× covers half; 2× covers twice. Other household earnings and actual days employed can differ.
matched_baskets_beijing.interpretation: A value of 1 covers one stated annual basket; 0.5 covers half; 2 covers two. Higher means greater affordability under those wage, price, household and workday assumptions; lower means less. Actual employment days, other household earnings, rationing and local price variation may differ. Adult and family baskets are not directly interchangeable.

historical_daily_baskets.meaning: This is how many daily subsistence baskets a published daily male unskilled construction wage could buy. It matches wages with the cost of a specified bundle of essentials.
historical_daily_baskets.calculation: Daily baskets affordable = daily wage ÷ price of one daily subsistence basket, using the source’s matched currency, locality and time. It is a published daily ratio; the Atlas does not turn it into an annual family budget by assuming days of employment.
historical_daily_baskets.interpretation: A value of 2 buys two stated daily baskets on a paid day; below 1 does not cover one. Higher means greater purchasing power for that wage and basket. It is not the household’s annual income, an average for every resident, or a value in international dollars.

wages_japan_real_index.meaning: This is Japan’s real-wage index: the source’s wage measure adjusted for its price index and expressed relative to 1932 = 100.
wages_japan_real_index.calculation: A real-wage series divides nominal pay by a compatible price index and rebases the result so the 1932 value is 100. The Atlas retains the published reconstruction and its occupational coverage.
wages_japan_real_index.interpretation: Above 100 means greater wage purchasing power than this series’ 1932 base; below 100 means less. A value of 120 means about 20% above that base, not 120 baskets or a comparable wage level in another country.

wages_japan_men.meaning: This is the published nominal daily wage for the men or women specified by the Japanese source, in yen per day.
wages_japan_men.calculation: The source compiles its daily pay measure for the stated worker group. The Atlas preserves the original nominal amount and source coverage; it does not adjust this measure for local prices or infer actual annual workdays.
wages_japan_men.interpretation: Higher means more yen of daily pay; lower means fewer. Inflation and differences in occupations or working hours can change the interpretation. These are worker-group averages or source measures, not necessarily equal-work comparisons or national household income.

wages_japan_women.meaning: This is the published nominal daily wage for the men or women specified by the Japanese source, in yen per day.

wages_japan_female_relative.meaning: This compares the source’s women’s daily pay with men’s daily pay, expressed as a percentage of men’s pay.
wages_japan_female_relative.calculation: Relative pay (%) = 100 × women’s daily wage ÷ men’s daily wage from the paired source year and units.
wages_japan_female_relative.interpretation: 100% means equal group pay; below 100% means women’s recorded pay is lower; above 100% means higher. This aggregate ratio is not adjusted for jobs, hours or other worker characteristics, so it is not a direct estimate of discrimination for equal work.

wages_angola_luanda_1.meaning: This is recorded daily compensation for Luanda · Unskilled African men, in the source’s nominal réis per day. The categories reflect historical records and are not present-day classifications.
wages_angola_luanda_1.calculation: The historical source reports or reconstructs pay for the named place and worker category. The Atlas keeps the original nominal unit and record scope; it does not assume that all residents received this wage or that coercive labour arrangements were freely negotiated.
wages_angola_luanda_1.interpretation: Higher means greater recorded daily compensation in that source unit, not necessarily greater purchasing power, freedom or wellbeing. Local prices, payment in kind, coercion, workdays and occupational differences matter.

wages_dakar_single_cost.meaning: This is a living-cost index for the household type named in Dakar · Single adult · living costs. It tracks the cost of the source’s household budget relative to Dakar in 1938 = 100.
wages_dakar_single_cost.calculation: Living-cost index = 100 × cost of the specified household budget in the selected year ÷ its cost in 1938, using the historical source’s prices, quantities and reconstruction.
wages_dakar_single_cost.interpretation: Above 100 means that budget costs more than in 1938; below 100 means less. It is a price index, not a basket affordability ratio or the cost in currency units. Household types use different budgets and are not uncertainty ranges.

wages_dakar_minimum_pay.meaning: This is the source’s nominal minimum-pay index for Dakar, relative to its 1938 level set to 100.
wages_dakar_minimum_pay.calculation: Minimum-pay index = 100 × nominal minimum pay in the selected year ÷ nominal minimum pay in 1938. The source’s official-wage and reconstruction conventions are retained.
wages_dakar_minimum_pay.interpretation: Above 100 means higher nominal minimum pay than the base year; below 100 means lower. Prices can change at the same time, so this is not a real-wage or affordability measure, and actual wages may differ from the official minimum.

wages_dakar_single_real.meaning: This is a real minimum-pay index for the household type in Dakar · Single adult · real minimum pay: minimum pay adjusted for its living costs, relative to 1938 = 100.
wages_dakar_single_real.calculation: Real minimum-pay index = 100 × nominal minimum-pay index ÷ the matching household living-cost index, with both based on 1938 = 100. The Atlas retains the author’s rounded historical reconstruction.
wages_dakar_single_real.interpretation: Above 100 means greater purchasing power than in 1938; below 100 means less. A value of 68 means 68% of base-year purchasing power, not 0.68 basic-needs baskets. The minimum wage may not have been universally paid and base-year needs were not necessarily met.
